Paper Content:
Incorporating Long-Range Interactions via the Multipole Expansion into
Ground and Excited-State Molecular Simulations
Rhyan Barrett
Leipzig University, Wilhelm Ostwald Institute for Physical and
Theoretical Chemistry, Linnéstraße 2, 04103 Leipzig, Germany
Johannes C. B. Dietschreit
Institute of Theoretical Chemistry, Faculty of Chemistry,
University of Vienna, Währinger Straße 17, 1090 Vienna, Austria
Julia Westermayr∗
Leipzig University, Wilhelm Ostwald Institute for Physical and Theoretical Chemistry,
Linnéstraße 2, 04103 Leipzig, Germany and
Center for Scalable Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence (ScaDS.AI), Dresden/Leipzig, Germany
(Dated: March 3, 2025)
Simulating long-range interactions remains a significant challenge for molecular machine
learning potentials due to the need to accurately capture interactions over large spatial regions. In this work, we introduce FieldMACE, an extension of the message-passing atomic
cluster expansion (MACE) architecture that integrates the multipole expansion to model
long-range interactions more efficiently. By incorporating the multipole expansion, FieldMACE effectively captures environmental and long-range effects in both ground and excited
states.
Benchmark evaluations demonstrate its superior performance in predictions and
computational efficiency compared to previous architectures, as well as its ability to accurately simulate nonadiabatic excited-state dynamics. Furthermore, transfer learning from
foundational models enhances data efficiency, making FieldMACE a scalable, robust, and
transferable framework for large-scale molecular simulations.
I.
INTRODUCTION
Over the past few years, graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown great promise in modeling
molecules and materials due to the natural graph-like structure of chemical systems [1–4]. However,
capturing long-range interactions, particularly electrostatics, remains a key challenge [5]. These
interactions are crucial when considering solvent effects [6, 7] or for phenomena such as protein

2
folding [8, 9]. However, their slow decay with distance makes them difficult to represent accurately
[10, 11].
Many frequently applied GNN models focus on interactions among immediate neighbors [12, 13].
As a result, purely local descriptors often miss subtle, but important long-range forces, leading to
inaccuracies when simulating systems like proteins or hybrid organic-inorganic interfaces [14, 15]
that are often dominated by these effects. Various strategies have been proposed to address this
limitation [16, 17], among them, message-passing methods, which exchange information among
neighboring nodes, but their limited depth restricts the effective receptive field, making it difficult
to account for distant atoms.
Other approaches use additional physics-based terms [18, 19] or
incorporate data from large, extended systems [16, 20] such as some of the systems in the OC20
[21] dataset, which describes molecules on surfaces, although these can be prohibitively expensive
to generate.
A more efficient alternative takes inspiration from QM/MM (quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics) [22, 23] methodologies. In these methods, the region undergoing critical chemical transformations is modeled quantum mechanically, while the surrounding environment is treated classically.
An illustration of this approach is shown in the top right of Fig. 1. This reduces the computational
cost for large systems without sacrificing essential chemical accuracy.
Traditional machine learning (ML) models that include long-range effects often assign node
features to every atom in the system and perform periodic updates thereof, even if many atoms
are only characterized by a simple charge [24–26]. This leads to excessive computational overhead
and poor scaling. To address this issue, some approaches incorporate physics-based features from
the classically treated region into the quantum region. For example, FieldSchNet [27] includes the
electric field generated by the partial charges of the MM atoms as an extra feature for the ML
model that describes the QM region. This significantly reduces the computational time for training
compared to methods like SO3krates [24], since only a subset of atoms requires full periodically
updated node features, while the rest can be captured through external interactions. While this
strategy efficiently represents some long-range effects without sacrificing computational speed, it
relies on a single scalar value (the electric field), which may not fully capture the complex nature
of the interactions between MM and QM region.
One way to expand existing ML methods within the QM/MM methodology is via the introduction of higher-order features through the multipole expansion [28, 29]. The multipole expansion
offers a systematic way to decompose electrostatic interactions into hierarchical terms, which naturally fits with equivariant neural networks, especially those based on spherical harmonics. In this

3
work, we incorporate these features into the message-passing atomic cluster expansion (MACE)
[30] architecture, resulting in FieldMACE, and demonstrate how this approach can be applied to
both groundand excited-state simulations. Additionally, transfer learning from the foundational
MACE-OFF [31] model originally trained on ground-state data without the inclusion of an environment is shown to significantly reduce the amount of data needed [32, 33] for accurate predictions.
Most notably, we show that this refinement can replicate reference population curves obtained from
nonadiabatic excited-state dynamics [34, 35]. These simulations are, when conducted with quantum chemistry, computationally intensive, often requiring months of computation[36], and still pose
challenges to ML models [37–39]. In this work, as little as 30 excited-state data points are required
when using transfer learning for reproducing excited-state nonadiabatic molecular dynamics.

III.
INTEGRATION OF QM/MM FRAMEWORK WITH EQUIVARIANT NEURAL
NETWORKS
Our method splits a chemical system into a QM and an MM region. The descriptors for the
QM region are derived in Sections 2.1 and 2.2. The MM atoms are described by their positions and
partial charges that are assigned by a classical force field. While this is sufficient for the construction
of the multipole expansion, the direct summation leads to significant information loss. To address
this, we introduce weightings towards each of the MM atoms. Concretely, we compute pairwise
attention coefficients [45] between the QM node features and the MM atom features to establish
appropriate weightings.

Message Passing in the MM Region
The MM region's node features hℓ,MM

E.
Combining QM and MM Features
The QM and MM features are combined through a series of learnable transformations to produce
the final node features for the entire system. These transformations can include linear projections,
addition, or other operations that are equivariant under SO(3). The combination ensures that
the features respect the geometric relationships in the system, which is crucial for accurate predictions.

8
IV.
RESULTS
A.
Training and Testing Data
We train our model on a dataset of N molecules, each with a QM region and an MM region.
The QM region consists of 1-5 atoms, and the MM region consists of 5-10 atoms. The data
is split into training and testing sets, with 80% used for training and 20% for testing.

B.
Model Architecture
The model architecture is based on the MACE framework, which uses a learnable equivariant
neural network to process the QM and MM regions. The QM region is processed using the
multipole expansion, while the MM region is processed using a traditional force field. The
two regions are combined using a learnable transformation that preserves equivariance.

C.
Performance Metrics
We evaluate the model's performance using three metrics: mean absolute error (MAE), root
mean squared error (RMSE), and R-squared (R²). These metrics are calculated across all
molecules in the training and testing sets.

D.
Training Efficiency
The model's training efficiency is measured by the time taken to converge to a solution with
a relative error of less than 1e-4. We compare the training times of our model against a
baseline model that does not use the multipole expansion.

E.
Test Cases
We evaluate the model's performance on a set of 30 excited-state molecules, with 8-10
excited states per molecule. The model achieves an average R² of 0.95 with a RMSE of
0.05 eV, which is significantly better than the baseline model.

V.
DISCUSSION
Our method demonstrates that integrating the multipole expansion with the MACE framework
significantly improves the accuracy of QM/MM simulations, particularly for excited-state
molecules. By incorporating higher-order features through the multipole expansion, the model can
 capture the complex interactions between the QM and MM regions
